summary: Defines how to send IPv6 packets over Master-Slave/Token-Passing networks, a medium access method on RS-485 wiring used in building automation. It covers the frame format and how to form link-local and autoconfigured addresses.

eli5.summary: Heating and lighting controls in buildings pass a talking token around. This explains how internet messages can ride along on that system.

questions: how does ipv6 run over ms/tp
what is frame type 34 in ms/tp
how is the ipv6 interface identifier formed on ms/tp
subtitle: How IPv6 packets ride on the token-passing RS-485 wiring used in building automation.

tldr.problem: Building automation devices talk over MS/TP, a token-passing protocol on RS-485 wiring, and had no standard way to carry IPv6 packets or to form IPv6 addresses.
tldr.mechanism: 6LoBAC puts compressed IPv6 packets (the 6LoWPAN LOWPAN_IPHC format) in MS/TP frames with Frame Type 34, and builds interface identifiers from the one-octet MAC address.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 can run directly on wired building controllers while coexisting with legacy MS/TP devices, which simply ignore the new frames.

today: RFC 8163 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2017. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Needs an MS/TP Profile
sections.content:
Master-Slave/Token-Passing (MS/TP) is a medium access control method for the RS-485 physical layer, used primarily in building automation networks. This RFC defines the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over it and the way to form link-local and statelessly autoconfigured IPv6 addresses. The specification is called 6LoBAC.

The approach adapts elements of the 6LoWPAN specifications (RFC 4944, RFC 6282 and RFC 6775) to constrained wired networks. MS/TP devices are typically low-cost microcontrollers with limited processing power and memory, low data rates and a small MAC address space, much like 6LoWPAN devices.

The RFC lists three differences from 6LoWPAN: MS/TP devices are typically mains powered, all devices on a segment can talk directly (no hidden nodes or mesh routing), and the latest MS/TP specification supports large payloads, so no fragmentation and reassembly is needed below IPv6.
sections.eli5: Building controllers are small, simple gadgets on a shared wire. This RFC teaches them to speak the internet's newer address language without changing how they already take turns.

sections.title: MS/TP and Its Frames
sections.content:
MS/TP builds multidrop networks over shielded twisted pair. Segments can reach up to 1000 meters at 115.2 kbit/s, or up to 1200 meters at lower bit rates. An interface needs only a UART, an RS-485 transceiver with a driver that can be disabled, and a 5 ms resolution timer, and the MAC is typically implemented in software.

Because RS-485 signaling needs a contention-free MAC, MS/TP uses a token. Only a master node holding the token can start sending data. After sending at most a configured maximum number of data frames, it passes the token to the next master, chosen by MAC address.

The newest MS/TP frames carry their data and a 32-bit CRC encoded with Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing (COBS). Encoding removes preamble patterns from the data, which fixes an old problem where preamble sequences inside data could cause lost frame synchronization. Frame Types 32 to 127 mark COBS-encoded frames, and ASHRAE assigned Frame Type 34 to IPv6 over MS/TP (LoBAC) encapsulation.

The Length field of a COBS-encoded frame is the size of the Encoded Data field plus three, so that legacy MS/TP devices ignore these frames.
sections.eli5: Only the kid holding the talking stick may speak, then they hand it on. The new kind of message is wrapped in a special way so older kids, who do not understand it, just ignore it.

sections.title: Profile, Constants and Goals
sections.content:
The main goals are to enable IPv6 directly on wired end devices in building automation and control networks using existing standards, and to coexist with legacy MS/TP implementations so networks can be upgraded step by step. To coexist, no changes are permitted to the MS/TP addressing modes, frame header format, control frames or Master Node state machine.

6LoBAC nodes are MS/TP master nodes that implement a Receive Frame state machine able to handle COBS-encoded frames. They MUST support 115.2 kbit/s and MAY support lower data rates. The RFC defines Nmin_COBS_length as 5 and Nmax_COBS_length as 1509 for the Length value, plus defaults of 1 for Nmax_info_frames and 127 for Nmax_master.
sections.eli5: The rule is to add the new trick without changing anything old devices rely on, so a building can be upgraded one device at a time.

sections.title: MAC Addresses, MTU and the LoBAC Layer
sections.content:
MS/TP MAC addresses are one octet long and assigned dynamically; each node on the link MUST have a unique one. Addresses 0 to 127 are valid for master nodes. Destination Address 255 means broadcast, and Source Address 255 MUST NOT be used. MS/TP has no multicast, so all IPv6 multicast packets MUST be broadcast at the MAC layer and filtered at the IPv6 layer.

IPv6 needs every link to have an MTU of at least 1280 octets. This specification defines an MTU of at least 1280 and at most 1500 octets, and recommends supporting 1500. MS/TP supports data units up to 2032 octets.

The LoBAC adaptation layer is a subset of the 6LoWPAN encapsulation, leaving out the Mesh, Broadcast, Fragmentation and LOWPAN_HC1 headers. The only defined format is a Dispatch value with bit pattern 01 1xxxxx followed by a LOWPAN_IPHC header and then the payload. Header compression MUST be implemented on all 6LoBAC nodes.
sections.eli5: Each device has a one-number name on the wire. Shouting to everyone is the only way to call a group, so each listener decides if the call was meant for them.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Address Mapping
sections.content:
A MAC-address-derived interface identifier is RECOMMENDED for link-local addresses, since it allows the most efficient header compression. It SHOULD be formed by concatenating the 8-bit MAC address to the seven octets 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xFF, 0xFE, 0x00, 0x00. For example, MAC address 0x4F gives the identifier shown in the RFC. This can never be all zeros. The link-local address is that identifier appended to FE80::/64.

For globally scoped addresses, a semantically opaque identifier with 64 bits of entropy is RECOMMENDED. A node that generates one MUST register it with its local routers using a Neighbor Solicitation with the Address Registration Option, as in RFC 6775. Prefixes used for stateless autoconfiguration MUST be 64 bits long.

Unicast address resolution follows RFC 4861. The Source/Target Link-Layer Address option has Length 1 and carries the 8-bit MS/TP address followed by zero padding. In compressed headers, a 16-bit address is the MS/TP address padded on the left with a zero octet, so multicast is shown as 0x00FF.
sections.eli5: Your internet address is built from your one-number name on the wire plus a fixed fill-in pattern, like adding a standard street name in front of your house number.

sections.title: Header Compression
sections.content:
6LoBAC REQUIRES LOWPAN_IPHC compression from RFC 6282, included by reference. Reading that RFC, replace "6LoWPAN" with "MS/TP network" and "IEEE 802.15.4 address" with "MS/TP address". Implementations MAY also support Generic Header Compression (RFC 7400) for transport headers.

If compression with context is used, the routers attached to the MS/TP segment MUST send the 6LoWPAN Context Option according to RFC 6775. The RFC also gives an example frame decode, with Frame Type 34 and an ICMPv6 echo request, and informative appendices on the abstract MAC interface, COBS and the CRC-32K.
sections.eli5: Because the wire is slow, the long internet header is squeezed into a short code, like writing a shorthand note both sides already know how to read.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 8065 for privacy threats faced by constrained nodes. Temporary addresses, typically used by clients, SHOULD be changed frequently to reduce correlation of activity, and nodes doing both client and server roles SHOULD support several addresses at once.

Globally scoped addresses containing MAC-derived identifiers may expose a network to address-scanning attacks. So the RFC recommends a 64-bit semantically opaque identifier for each globally scoped address, generated by methods such as those in RFC 7217 or RFC 4941. IANA actions are none, because the document uses values already reserved by RFC 4944 and RFC 6282.
sections.eli5: If your address is easy to guess from your name tag, snoops can find you. So for talking to the wider world, use a random-looking address instead.
